lines.t: Are you actually bad with money, or did nobody ever teach you how it works?
Most of us never sat through a class on interest, inflation, or emergency funds.
Then we blamed ourselves for every mistake that followed.
In six minutes, I will show you what the data says, and three small habits to start with.
Let's begin with a test.
Every few years, the FINRA Foundation measures how well American adults understand basic money ideas.
In its 2024 survey, respondents answered seven financial knowledge questions.
Only 27 percent got at least five of the seven right.
That is nearly the same as the 28 percent in 2021.
So roughly three in four adults missed three or more of the seven questions.
There is one bright spot in the results.
One question asked about inflation, and 58 percent of respondents answered it correctly, up from 53 percent in 2021.
Among adults aged 18 to 34, that score rose from 34 percent to 44 percent.
That hints that people can learn these ideas when they get the chance.
Knowledge is not fixed, and that is good news.
Now ask where most people were supposed to learn this.
In February 2024, the Council for Economic Education reported that 35 states require a personal finance course to graduate high school.
That is up by 12 states since 2022.
Only 15 states require a full semester-long course, which the council calls its highest standard.
These rules are growing quickly, so plenty of adults finished school before they existed.
A 2026 national report card on personal finance education puts the speed of change in perspective.
In 2013, only three states earned an A grade, covering just 5 percent of students.
By 2031, the report projects that 29 states will require a standalone personal finance course.
It also projects that 73 percent of public high school students graduating in 2031 will take a substantive course.
Progress is real, but it is recent.
Here is what people say about it.
In a 2025 poll cited in that report card, 83 percent of U.S. adults said their state should require a semester-long or year-long course.
And 82 percent of respondents who attended high school said they wish they had been required to take a personal finance class.
Those answers do not sound like people who feel lazy or careless.
They point to a gap in what people were taught.
A gap in knowledge can show up in everyday life.
In the FINRA Foundation's 2024 study, 46 percent of adults said they had set aside three months of living expenses.
That is down from 53 percent in 2021.
The study also found that 53 percent always pay their credit cards in full each month, down six percentage points from 2021.
Many forces sit behind those numbers, including higher costs, so knowledge is only part of the story.
But it is a part you can change.
So let's change the question.
Being bad with money sounds like a personality trait, as if you were born without the talent.
It is much closer to a skill, like driving or cooking.
Nobody is born knowing how to read a lease or compare loan offers.
People learn those skills from teachers, practice, and mistakes.
If you never had the teacher, the mistakes are not proof that something is wrong with you.
That is not an excuse to stop. It is a reason to start.
Habit one: learn one idea at a time.
Pick a single concept this week, such as compound interest, inflation, or what an emergency fund is for.
Spend fifteen minutes on a trustworthy source, like the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau website.
Then write one sentence in your own words explaining it.
If you can explain it simply, you probably understand it.
Do that for a few months, and money questions stop feeling like tricks.
Habit two: let a machine do the remembering.
Willpower is unreliable, especially at the end of a long week.
Set up an automatic transfer to savings on payday, even a small one.
For example, if you are paid every two weeks and move $25 each time, that adds up to $650 in a year.
That is an illustration, and any amount you can keep up is the right amount.
The goal is to build the habit before you build the balance.
Habit three: look at your money once a month.
Set a calendar reminder and spend ten minutes, no more.
Check three numbers: what came in, what went out, and what is left in savings.
You are not judging yourself, you are collecting information.
Avoiding the numbers feels safer, but that is how small problems grow quietly.
Looking is the habit that makes the other two habits work.
So, are you actually bad with money?
The data says most adults missed several basic questions, and school rules are only now catching up.
That points to a teaching gap, not to a flaw in you.
Nobody was born knowing how money works, and nobody teaches it by accident.
So start with one idea, one automatic transfer, and one monthly check.
Real results vary, and this video is for education only, not personal financial advice. Talk to a licensed professional before big decisions.
